tagline: Highway 2 links farm country, oilfield remnants and a former commune.
intro: The Boom or Bust Byway follows Highway 2 through Caddo, Bossier, Webster and Claiborne parishes, between the Texas border area and Lake Claiborne. At the western end, the two-lane road bends past the tip of Caddo Lake. Boom or Bust Byway highlights farm crops, roadside trees and disused oilfield equipment. National Scenic Byway designation followed in 2021. The route explores the changing fortunes of oil and gas, lumber, transportation, farming and entertainment.

Highway 2 took its number in Louisiana’s 1955 highway renumbering. It originally entered Homer’s courthouse square, but a northern bypass opened in 1964. In the early 1970s, another change sent the road through Shongaloo before turning toward Leton. Parts of older alignments survive as local roads, including Old Homer Road near Blackburn and Old Lisbon Road at LA 806.

Travel east from the Caddo Lake area through Vivian and Hosston, then cross the Red River into Bossier Parish. Plain Dealing, Sarepta and Shongaloo follow before the road turns toward Homer. At Plain Dealing, the road briefly widens to four lanes before narrowing again as it leaves town with LA 157. Germantown Colony lies on a separate excursion north of Minden. Beyond Homer, Highway 2 passes the northern end of Lake Claiborne.

moments.title: Caddo Lake
moments.text: Flooded cypress forest is part of Caddo Lake’s wetland landscape on the Texas–Louisiana border. Before oil, riverboat ports served the lake. Removal of logjams lowered its water level by more than ten feet, reducing navigability and undermining the East Texas ports. In 1911, Gulf Refining Company erected the Ferry Lake No. 1 oil platform here. Derricks spread across the lake, damaging its ecosystem, before the industry moved to richer fields in Texas. Protection expanded in 1993 when Caddo Lake became a Ramsar wetland, part of an international effort to protect important wetlands.

moments.title: Germantown Colony
moments.text: Dovetailed corners join the hewn logs of Countess Leon’s home and the kitchen-dining hall at Germantown. Elisa Leon led the founding of the German religious community in 1836. Its community of about thirty-five people held property in common and followed religious principles. Civil War privation and the colony’s pacifism contributed to the hardships that preceded its end as a commune in 1871. The two surviving buildings have replacement windows, and none of their porches are original. Most of the colony’s houses, barns, stores and shops have disappeared. The kitchen-dining hall retains a stone cellar beneath its log construction.

moments.title: Homer
moments.text: Homer’s 1860 brick courthouse predates the oil boom that brought guests to the Claiborne Hotel across the square. Oil discoveries at Homer and Haynesville in 1921 began a boom that continued through the 1930s. The former hotel houses the Herbert S. Ford Memorial Museum. Its exhibits place a compressed cotton bale beside a replica oilfield laborer. A recording follows a Mississippi farm family’s move to Claiborne Parish for opportunities in oil and gas. The museum has housed Ford’s collection in the former hotel since 1982; the collection itself began in 1924 and previously occupied several locations.
